questions.stem: Why are the solutions mixed in an insulated container?

options.text: To prevent heat loss so the temperature change reflects the reaction alone
options.explanation: Insulation keeps the released heat inside the vessel, so the thermometer sees the full change.

options.text: To speed up the reaction between the two solutions
options.explanation: Insulation changes where the heat goes, not how fast the chemicals react.

options.text: To keep the solutions at a constant temperature
options.explanation: The temperature is meant to change; insulation only stops that change leaking away.

options.text: To stop the solutions mixing too quickly
options.explanation: Mixing is required and is helped by stirring, not prevented.

questions.stem: Which set of reactions can be studied by solution calorimetry of this kind?

options.text: Neutralisation, dissolving and displacement
options.explanation: All three happen in solution and release or absorb a measurable amount of heat.

options.text: Combustion, dissolving and neutralisation
options.explanation: Combustion needs a burning fuel and a different arrangement with a spirit burner.

options.text: Combustion, displacement and rusting
options.explanation: Combustion uses the copper-can method, and rusting is far too slow to measure this way.

options.text: Electrolysis, dissolving and neutralisation
options.explanation: Electrolysis needs a power supply and is not one of the solution-mixing examples.

questions.stem: In the method, why is an excess of the second reagent added?

options.text: So that all of the first reagent reacts and the temperature rise reaches its maximum
options.explanation: Excess second reagent drives the reaction to completion, giving the largest measurable temperature change.

options.text: To make the solution less dense so it is easier to stir
options.explanation: Density is assumed equal to water; stirring is for even mixing, not density control.

options.text: To keep the temperature constant during the reaction
options.explanation: The temperature is supposed to rise; excess reagent maximises that rise.

options.text: To prevent heat escaping through the cup walls
options.explanation: Insulation and a lid slow heat escape; excess reagent has a different job.

questions.stem: Which assumption lets the calculation treat the solution as if it were pure water?

options.text: The solution has the same specific heat capacity and density as water
options.explanation: Taking 4.18 J/g/°C and 1 g/cm3 lets the mass heated be read straight from the volume.

options.text: The solution boils at exactly 100 °C
options.explanation: Boiling point is not part of the assumption set for these calculations.

options.text: The solution is colourless so the thermometer can be read
options.explanation: Colour does not enter the calculation at all.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic in every case
options.explanation: The method covers exothermic and endothermic changes alike.

questions.stem: A polystyrene cup, a vacuum flask and a metal can are all acceptable because they all…

options.text: act as the calorimeter holding the reacting mixture
options.explanation: Each vessel can serve as the insulated container whose contents are measured.

options.text: measure the temperature directly
options.explanation: The thermometer measures temperature; the vessel just holds the mixture.

options.text: burn the fuel cleanly
options.explanation: Burning belongs to the combustion experiment with a spirit burner, not to solution mixing.

options.text: stop the reaction from completing
options.explanation: The assumption list says the reaction is complete; the vessel does not hinder it.

questions.stem: State the measurement used to find the energy produced when two solutions react.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature change is measured as the solutions are mixed, and from it the energy produced is found.

questions.stem: State two simple containers that can serve as a calorimeter.
questions.modelAnswer: A polystyrene cup, a vacuum flask or a metal can can all serve as a simple calorimeter.

questions.stem: Explain the purpose of the insulation around the container in solution calorimetry.
questions.modelAnswer: Insulation prevents heat loss to the surroundings, so the temperature change recorded belongs to the reaction alone.

questions.stem: A student assumes the solution's density is 1 g/cm3 to estimate its mass from its volume. State the other standard assumptions about heat in this method.
questions.modelAnswer: The method assumes the specific heat capacity is 4.18 J/g/°C and that heat losses to the surroundings are negligible.

questions.stem: Why is the spirit burner weighed before and after the experiment?

options.text: To find the mass of fuel burned during the temperature rise
options.explanation: The mass lost by the burner is the fuel consumed, which pairs the energy change with the amount of fuel.

options.text: To check the balance is working correctly
options.explanation: The balance is assumed fine; the two weighings measure fuel used.

options.text: To measure the temperature of the flame
options.explanation: A balance cannot read temperature; the thermometer does that.

options.text: To confirm the wick stayed dry throughout
options.explanation: Wick condition is not the target measurement; fuel mass is.

questions.stem: Why is the flame extinguished after the temperature has risen by roughly 20 °C?

options.text: To give a measurable rise while keeping heat losses and fuel use under control
options.explanation: A rise of about 20 °C is large enough to read accurately yet short enough to limit uncontrolled losses.

options.text: Because water cannot be heated by more than 20 °C
options.explanation: Water can heat further; the value is a working choice, not a physical limit.

options.text: Because the spirit burner stops working above that temperature
options.explanation: The burner could keep burning; the stop is deliberate.

options.text: To make sure the fuel is all used up
options.explanation: The burner must still hold fuel for the final weighing to show the mass burned.

questions.stem: Which pair names the main sources of error in the combustion experiment?

options.text: Heat losses and incomplete combustion
options.explanation: Heat escapes to the surroundings and some fuel burns incompletely, both shrinking the measured effect.

options.text: Heat gains and complete combustion
options.explanation: Complete combustion is the ideal, not an error; gains are not the named problem.

options.text: Thermometer drift and balance drift
options.explanation: Instrument drift is not one of the two named errors for this experiment.

options.text: Water evaporating and the can rusting
options.explanation: Neither evaporation nor rust is the named error pair.

questions.stem: How does a lid reduce the error in the measured energy change?

options.text: It prevents heat escaping from the water surface into the air
options.explanation: A lid sits over the calorimeter so rising warm water loses less heat to the air above.

options.text: It raises the flame temperature of the burner
options.explanation: The lid does not touch the flame; it caps the can.

options.text: It stops the water from evaporating completely
options.explanation: Evaporation control is incidental; the named purpose is heat loss.

options.text: It makes the combustion reaction complete
options.explanation: Completeness of burning depends on oxygen supply at the wick, not on the lid over the water.

questions.stem: Not all the heat from the burning fuel reaches the water. Where does the rest go?

options.text: Some is lost to the surroundings and some is absorbed by the calorimeter
options.explanation: Those two sinks are the named destinations for the missing heat.

options.text: It is destroyed inside the flame
options.explanation: Energy is conserved; it spreads to other places instead of vanishing.

options.text: It turns the fuel into a denser liquid
options.explanation: Density changes of the fuel are not part of the heat account.

options.text: It stays in the wick forever
options.explanation: The wick is not a named heat sink in this experiment.

questions.stem: State how the fuel is weighed in the combustion practical.
questions.modelAnswer: A spirit burner with the fuel is weighed before and after the run to find how much fuel burned.

questions.stem: State the temperature rise at which the flame is put out in the combustion experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The flame is extinguished once the water has risen by about 20 degrees Celsius, and the final temperature is recorded.

questions.stem: Explain why the measured temperature rise understates the true energy released by the burning fuel.
questions.modelAnswer: Heat escapes to the surroundings and some fuel burns incompletely, so the water receives less energy than the combustion actually released.

questions.stem: A student's flame flickers in a draught. State the two simple defences against this error source.
questions.modelAnswer: A lid over the calorimeter and shielding from draughts reduce the heat lost to the surroundings.
